# A Map of AI-for-Architecture Work {#sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map}

::: {.abstract}
This appendix consolidates the prior body of AI-for-architecture work that Architecture 2.0 builds on. It groups established results into families, maps each family to the principal life-cycle stages for which the cited work demonstrates activity and to the chapter that develops it, and states how the discipline in this book differs from any single family. The map is a reading aid and a positioning statement, not a survey.
:::

Machine learning has appeared in computer architecture for decades. Early work proposed learned in-chip mechanisms and models of architecture design spaces. More recent systems couple learned methods to simulators, compilers, and implementation tools. The families below are the strands this material draws on. Collecting them serves a narrow purpose. It is not another survey, which existing work already provides [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture], but a positioning aid that shows what each family contributes, which principal life-cycle stages the cited work demonstrates, and where this book puts it to use (@tbl-ai-arch-map).

Most method families in the table fall into three regimes, and each regime supports a different claim. Learned in-chip components occupy the mechanism regime and are judged within the mechanism's own budget, such as mispredict rate at fixed storage and latency. Learned cost models occupy the design-space-model regime and are judged by predictive fidelity against the tool they approximate. Families that participate in the design process itself occupy the third regime. Benchmarks and datasets sit alongside these regimes as supporting evaluation infrastructure. This book takes the normative position that a complete third-regime result must be judged at the level of the architecture study, not from the generated artifact alone. Confusing the regimes allows a bounded branch-prediction result to become evidence for trusting an agent with a floorplan, which it is not.

| **Family of work** | **Representative results** | **Principal life-cycle stages demonstrated** | **Developed in** | **Key sources** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned in-chip components** | Perceptron branch predictors and learned prefetchers, where learning is embedded in the mechanism itself and does a bounded tactical job | Implement, Evaluate | @sec-moonshot, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture] |
| **Learned cost models and predictive DSE** | Surrogates and regression models that predict performance and power across a design space from cheap features | Explore, Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] |

| **Benchmarks and datasets** | QuArch tests architecture knowledge through question answering | Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect | [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch] |

: **The unit of work in Architecture 2.0 is the architecture study and its reviewable claim, not any single family's artifact:** each row names prior results, the principal life-cycle stages demonstrated by the cited work, and the chapters that develop it. The stage column uses only the six labels defined in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. {#tbl-ai-arch-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,15,22,15]"}

These families are not exclusive. An agentic design-space search may call a learned cost model, invoke an autoscheduler, and emit RTL, meaning a single study can touch several rows at once.

The learned in-chip components family carries a filter the others do not. A proposed component is useful only when inference fits the mechanism's storage and latency budget. The perceptron predictor provides a bounded example, with a 4\ KB hardware budget and a prediction available within one cycle [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron]. This result ties predictive accuracy to the resources consumed inside the mechanism.

The families also occupy distinct regions of the territory drawn in @fig-book-composition. The learned-components, cost-model, autotuning, and co-design families live where architecture meets ML. Reinforcement learning for physical design and LLM-driven RTL generation live where ML meets EDA. Kahng describes learned models that use earlier-stage features to predict routing hotspots and downstream-flow outcomes [@Kahng2018Machine]. These surrogates are the cost-model family applied to physical design, where a cheap prediction can guide an iteration before a more expensive downstream flow runs. Generated assertions and testbenches span the two regions, but they remain candidate verification collateral that requires independent execution and review [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @QiuEtAl2024AutoBench; @KangEtAl2024FVEval]. As the corresponding rows in @tbl-ai-arch-map show, AgentDSE places tool feedback inside exploration, while QuArch contributes an Evaluate-stage test of architecture knowledge and question answering.

Reading down the stage column shows a related asymmetry. Explore appears in five rows, Implement in six, and Evaluate in five. No row demonstrates Formulate, Interpret and Explain, or Review and Decide. This book adds those responsibilities to its normative standard for a complete architecture study.

Because these methods often combine, what separates Architecture 2.0 from any single family is its unit of work. A learned branch predictor changes one mechanism. A macro-placement agent proposes a candidate for one implementation step. An RTL-generating model produces one artifact. Each result is judged on that bounded output.

This material instead takes the architecture study and its reviewable claim as the unit. The question is not just whether a model produced a plausible artifact, but whether the whole loop, from intent through tools to evidence, supports an architectural decision that another architect can inspect and challenge. The families mapped here supply the methods; the discipline supplies the standard of judgment that decides what their outputs are worth.

## Candidates, Not Decisions

Those outputs are always candidates, not decisions. An autoscheduler's proposed schedule supports a performance claim only after measured execution on the relevant hardware. A proposed placement requires downstream place-and-route, timing, power, and congestion checks. Generated RTL requires functional and implementation checks. Qualified people in the accountable organization retain acceptance, while verification and implementation owners retain signoff for their domains.

Candidates can mislead through false confidence or hidden total cost. Generated assertions can pass vacuously while checking nothing that matters, so their apparent success is not independent evidence [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking] (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When assessing macro-placement methods such as AlphaChip, a total-cost comparison includes the pretraining and fine-tuning runs actually used for the reported design, together with their compute [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Neither apparent verification success nor a favorable cost comparison replaces the required acceptance and signoff.
